Madagascar Recalls 2017 Rift Valley Fever Outbreak and Its Economic Toll

Antananarivo – Seven years after the 2017 Rift Valley Fever outbreak that prompted widespread health measures and significant economic disruption across Madagascar, officials and analysts are reflecting on the lessons learned from the crisis.

Between February and May 2017, Madagascar faced its largest outbreak of Rift Valley Fever in decades. The mosquito-borne virus, which affects both livestock and humans, led to nearly 400 confirmed human cases and at least 30 deaths, according to figures released by the Ministry of Public Health at the time. In a bid to contain the spread, the government imposed temporary livestock market closures, restricted inter-regional travel, and suspended large public gatherings in several affected provinces.

These emergency measures had a profound effect on economic activity nationwide. While the epidemic was concentrated in the regions of Alaotra-Mangoro, Sofia, and Betsiboka, restrictions rippled across the country, impacting transportation, agriculture, and trade.

“Market closures and transport bans hit small farmers hardest,” recalled Patrice Andrianarisoa, spokesperson for the Malagasy Rural Producers Union. “Many families rely on selling zebu and goats at weekly markets. With those shut, incomes dried up almost overnight.” According to the union, rural incomes dropped by as much as 40% in some districts during the height of the outbreak.

The shutdown also affected the country’s vital vanilla and clove exports. “With movement restrictions, getting crops to port was much more difficult,” said Lanto Raharisoa, an analyst at Esaka Economic Research. “Export volumes for April and May 2017 were down 17% compared to the previous year.”

Urban businesses, too, felt the consequences. The urban transport network in Antananarivo operated at reduced capacity, and hotels reported a wave of cancellations as domestic and regional travel slowed. “It was a very difficult period for service industries,” said Fanja Rakotomalala, manager of the Hotel Manjakamiadana.

The government responded with emergency food relief in the hardest-hit zones and a vaccination campaign targeting livestock. Public Health Minister Dr. Jean-Claude Razafindrakoto later credited swift action with preventing a wider health disaster. “Our priority was saving lives, but we recognize the economic sacrifices made by so many Malagasy families,” he said in a recent interview.

Today, no such disruptions remain, and trade groups say the experience has prompted better epidemic preparedness and improved disease surveillance in livestock markets. “We are more resilient now,” said Andrianarisoa. “But we hope never to face such a crisis again.”
